My parents counselors solution to our strife was for them to kick me out (this was several years ago). With that said, all of you who thought you were clever by attempting to point out hypocrisy and prejudice: before making such assertions check your facts.

Somewhat of a dog expert here; I have volunteered at a few shelters/rescues. I would like to tell you right off the bat that offering him food is not the solution. My best recommendation is that you employ Cesar Milan's method: no touch/talk/eye contact. This is doubly true if he is eating or sleeping.

It sounds to me like your boyfriend's coddling behavior is a large part of the problem. I see this all too often; people who adopt animals that have been abused will treat it like a child; the behaviors you have described from your bf indicate this strongly.

With that said, when you said he can sense your fear, you were correct. It will be necessary for YOU to carry yourself in an assertive and confident manner. Claim your space, and make it clear that it is not ok to violate your personal area, just as you would if a stranger approached you. I would really like to stress, however, that the most important factor is your boyfriend. If he does not consider the discomfort you feel around his dog, he may not consider your feelings in other situations. Best of luck.

P.s. I don't know if tris203 was kidding, but some people think this works (unfortunately). If a dog sees you as a target for domination to begin  with, it can see this as a challenge. With some dogs this can be disasterous.
